transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is that I keep making these small mistakes that I really should be catching. They’re not huge disasters, but they’re the kind of things that make me stop and think, “Why did I do that?”

Like at the senior center, I’ll write down the wrong time on a class sheet even though the correct time is right there in front of me, and then I have to go back and fix it or someone points it out. Or if I’m doing something at home, like measuring a board, I’ll measure it once and think I’ve got it, but then I cut it just a hair short because I skipped over some small print or didn’t really take in the detail I was supposed to notice.

It’s frustrating, because I’m not trying to be careless. I feel like I’m looking right at the thing, but somehow I miss the little part that matters.
Are these kinds of mistakes happening in other areas of your life, or do they seem to be limited to places like the senior center or when you’re working on something at home?

It’s mostly those kinds of situations, I’d say—where there are little details right in front of me and I somehow don’t catch them. The senior center is one place it shows up, because I’ll be filling out something like a class sheet, and I’ll put down the wrong time even though the correct time is sitting there on the schedule or whatever paper I’m using. Then I look back and think, “How did I miss that?”

And at home it’s similar, just with different things. Like if I’m measuring a board, I’ll measure it once and feel like I’ve got it, but then I cut it a little short because I skipped over some small mark or didn’t really take in the fine print on the tape or the instructions. It’s not that I don’t care—it’s more like my eyes pass over it but my brain doesn’t grab onto it.

So I don’t know if I’d say it’s only those places, but those are the clearest examples. It’s the little accuracy things that keep getting me.
Have you noticed these kinds of attention or accuracy problems before, or is this something that’s fairly new?

No, it’s not completely new. I mean, the particular mistakes now are adult things, obviously, but when I think back, there were signs of this even when I was a kid.

In elementary school, I remember my teachers would say I was bright, that I understood things, but then on the report cards or in notes home there’d always be something like, “forgets his books,” or “lost his homework,” or “needs reminders to stay on task.” I’d have the homework done sometimes and then somehow not turn it in, or I’d leave the book I needed at school or at home, whichever was the wrong place.

And I can remember staring out the window during class—not trying to be difficult, just sort of drifting—until the teacher said my name or came by my desk. If someone kept me on track, I could do the work, but left on my own I’d kind of wander off mentally. So I guess the accuracy problems feel more noticeable now, but the pattern of missing things or needing someone to pull me back has been there a long time.
Have you noticed these attention and accuracy problems getting worse over time, or have they stayed about the same since you were a child?

I’d say it’s been there in some form for a long time, but it’s been more noticeably interfering since we moved into the condo, which was about… a year and a month ago now.

Before that, I could kind of work around it, or maybe I didn’t notice it as much because things were more familiar. But after the move, there were more details to keep track of, and that’s when I started feeling like, “Okay, this is actually getting in my way.” Not every single day in some dramatic way, but enough that it’s been standing out to me more than it used to.
Have you noticed any problems with your memory, like forgetting things more often than usual, getting lost in familiar places, or having trouble finding the right words when you're trying to talk?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re describing, anyway. I mean, I forget things in the sense of misplacing something or walking into a room and having to pause for a second, but I feel like everybody does that some. I haven’t been getting lost in places I know, no. If I’m driving somewhere familiar or going around the neighborhood, I know where I am.

And with words, I might have that normal thing where a name is on the tip of my tongue and then it comes back later, but I haven’t noticed myself not being able to talk or losing words in a way that scares me. My wife hasn’t said anything like that either, at least not that I can think of.

So I’d say no, not really. It’s more that I miss details or don’t keep track of something right in the moment, not that my memory feels like it’s disappearing.
Have you ever found yourself acting on impulse without thinking things through, or feeling unusually restless or fidgety, especially in situations where you're expected to sit still or focus?

Yeah… I wouldn’t say I’m a big risk-taker or anything like that, but the restless part, yes, I do notice that.

Like if I have to sit through a whole meeting, or even just a quiet evening at the condo, I’ll start to get this kind of ants-in-my-pants feeling. It’s not always obvious on the outside, I don’t think, but inside I’m sort of itching to get up. I’ll want to check something, or go look at something in another room, or putter around with some little task that probably doesn’t need doing right then.

Sometimes I can sit still if I really have to, but it takes effort. I’ll be shifting around or thinking, “Okay, how much longer is this?” And at home, if it’s quiet and I’m supposed to just relax, I’ll still find myself getting up to check a door, move something, straighten something, whatever. It’s like my body wants to be doing something even when there isn’t really anything important to do.
Have you found that these issues with attention and restlessness interfere with your ability to function in more than one area of your life, such as work, home, or social situations?

Yes, I think it does, in more than one place. It’s not like my whole life is falling apart, but it causes enough little problems that I’ve had to change what I take on.

For example, I used to help lead a couple of DIY-type workshops, and after some mix-ups — not huge disasters, but enough wrong details or missed steps that it made me uncomfortable — I kind of stepped back from being in that lead role. I didn’t want to be the person throwing things off or making everyone else have to fix it after me.

And at home, my wife has had to double-check plans more than she used to. Like if we’re coordinating family visits or something going on at the center, she’ll go back over the times or the details because I might get something crossed up and then it affects other people. That part bothers me, because I don’t want her to feel like she has to supervise me, you know? But realistically, her checking has probably prevented me from messing up plans more than once.
Looking back, were you noticeably more distracted, restless, or prone to making careless mistakes compared to other children your age before you turned 12?

Yes… looking back, I think so. I mean, it’s hard to judge yourself as a kid from this far away, but I do remember that being a theme even in elementary school.

My teachers would write things like I was bright, or that I understood the material, but then there’d always be some comment about not bringing the right book, or losing homework, or needing reminders to stay on task. I can picture those report card notes — not word for word, but that general “he’s capable, but…” kind of thing.

And I did a lot of staring out the window, honestly. If the teacher was talking and someone wasn’t keeping me pointed at what I was supposed to be doing, my mind would just go somewhere else. It wasn’t that I was trying to be difficult. I just sort of drifted, and then I’d realize I’d missed instructions or I didn’t have what I needed.

So, yes, compared to other kids, I think I probably was more like that before 12. Not wild or anything, but distracted and careless with school stuff, definitely.
Can you recall if these symptoms of being distracted, restless, or making careless mistakes started before age 12 and have continued into your adulthood?

Yes, that sounds right. I can’t put an exact age on it, but definitely before 12 — elementary school, really.

I remember teachers saying I was bright, like I understood things well enough, but then the comments would be about the practical stuff: forgetting the right books, losing homework, not having things turned in, or needing someone to keep me on track. And I did a lot of staring out the window. I can still picture that, just sort of drifting off while the teacher was talking, and then realizing I’d missed what I was supposed to be doing.

So it wasn’t something that just showed up later in life. It was there when I was a kid, and in one form or another it’s kind of followed me into adulthood.
